WELCOME

**Thank you for purchasing OXI Coral.**

The introduction of the Mutable Instruments Plaits module was a revolution in compact, multi-engine synth voices. Coral builds on those open-source foundations. It packs 8 independent voices into a 14 HP module. Each voice has its own envelopes, filter and effects. The interface is colourful and organic. On top of that you get custom wavetables and a sample playback engine per voice.

But Coral is not just another polyphonic synth. The multipart concept lets you arrange the 8 voices however you like: 8 monophonic parts, one 8-voice polyphonic part, or any combination. A single Coral can be a polysynth, a drum machine, a groovebox and a sound-exploration module at the same time.

Coral firmware 3.0 introduces a new way of building your instrument. Instead of a handful of fixed engine sets, there are now 27 engines and you choose any 10 of them. The web Firmware Updater compiles that exact selection and flashes it to your Coral over USB. This manual covers that workflow, the new engines, the on-device options menu, and the companion web apps.

**The OXI team**

1　OVERVIEW

Coral is a polyphonic, multipart synthesizer voice module for Eurorack. It is polyphonic: it plays up to 8 notes at once. It is multipart: each of the 8 voices runs its own engine, listens to its own MIDI channel, and holds its own parameter values.

The simplest way to play Coral is as an 8-voice polyphonic MIDI synth. You can also play it as a single voice from CV. That is how it behaves the first time you power it on. To hear how Coral sounds, patch a Gate and a CV/Oct pair. These trigger the internal envelopes.

1.1 Specifications

Dimensions　14 HP, 3 cm deep

Panel　Black anodized aluminium with colour silkprint

Consumption　+12V: 110 mA · -12V: 10 mA · +5V: 0 mA

Outputs　2x mono DC-coupled outputs (±5 V), used as a stereo pair

Inputs　1x MIDI TRS (Type A and B compatible) · 8x CV inputs ±5 V (±10 V max) · 1x Gate input

Storage　Micro SD card, always in the slot. Class 10 / 70 MB/s or faster for heavy sampler use

1.3 Powering Up

1. Make sure the factory Micro SD card is inserted.

2. Mount Coral in a powered Eurorack case with the ribbon cable oriented correctly (red stripe to -12V).

3. Power on. The LED ring shows voice activity in the main view.

4. Send notes on MIDI channel 1. You can also patch a Gate to the trigger input and a CV to the OCT input. Then play.

NOTE By default all 8 voices listen to MIDI channel 1 and are assigned as one part. This is the best starting point.

1.4 Signal Flow

Figure 1.2. Per-voice signal chain. Engine and Noise go into the Filter, then the Amp, then Pan. The Mod and Amp envelopes shape the Filter and the Amp. Each voice has its own Chorus insert. The Limiter sums all 8 voices. The Space reverb is a send and return, then the stereo output.

Each voice runs its engine and an independent noise source through a low-pass filter and an amplifier. The Mod and Amp envelopes shape it. Coral then pans it. The chorus works per voice. A limiter sums all voices. The Space (reverb) engine is a shared send. The result reaches the stereo output.

2　INTERFACE AND PLAYING

This chapter covers the main view and the pots, which have two functions each. It also covers engine selection, the encoder click cycle, presets, the options menu and the randomizer.

2.1 Main View

In the main view the LED ring shows the amplitude of each active voice. This is the default screen; turning any pot returns you here from any menu.

Figure 2.1. Main view, voice status: voices 1, 2, 4 and 6 active.

2.2 Primary and Secondary Parameters

Each pot controls one main parameter and one secondary parameter. This lets Coral pack a lot of control into a small panel. To change a secondary parameter, push and hold the encoder (this acts as SHIFT) and turn the corresponding pot.

The pot position and the stored value may not match, so to avoid sudden jumps you first have to catch up the stored value. This applies to both main and secondary parameters. For a primary parameter the stored value is shown in the section colour and the pot position in white. For a secondary parameter the stored value is white and the current position is orange.

NOTE At start-up the pot position and the stored value may not match. You may then need to catch up the main or secondary values.

Taking control back from MIDI

The same idea applies when something else is driving Coral. A sequencer or DAW can move a parameter with a MIDI CC. The pot then no longer matches the sound. The pot must catch up before it takes control again. As you turn, the pot and the value meet in the middle. Control passes smoothly, without a jump. The same happens when you switch part or load a preset.

It applies to every parameter a CC can reach, on both layers:

• Main functions: HARM, TIMBRE, MORPH, FILTER cutoff, F.RESO, F.ENV, AMP ATK, AMP DR, MOD ATK, MOD DR and SUST.

• Secondary functions: Level, Pan, Noise, Space (reverb) send, Delay send, and Chorus send or HP cutoff.

Figure 2.2. Engine-selection ring: 10 engine slots around the ring, the active slot lit pink, remaining slots dim. Slot contents depend on the firmware you built.

NOTE Your 10 engine slots are whatever you chose in the Firmware Updater (Chapter 9). The example rings in this manual are just one possible layout.

What happens to your sound when you switch engine

Every engine on a part keeps its own tone settings. Move to another engine and come back. That engine returns exactly as you left it. It keeps HARM, TIMBRE and MORPH, the filter cutoff, the filter envelope and resonance, both envelopes, sustain and noise.

Your effects mix does not move. The Space (reverb), Delay and Chorus sends belong to the part, not to the engine. The HP filter cutoff does too. Set a reverb and delay balance you like. You can then change engines on stage. The mix stays put and the delay keeps running.

TIP This is what makes engine switching usable on stage. Set the send levels once for the part.

You can then move through engines without the effects jumping or dropping out.

2.6 Presets

You can save and load all parameters and the full voice configuration in 10 preset slots. The extended-presets option gives you 100 (Chapter 8). Everything is stored, so a preset recalls exactly as you left it. Presets can also be recalled with MIDI Program Change messages.

Tap the encoder to jump between screens. Turning the encoder in any screen enters selection mode, so the next tap confirms. Turn any pot to exit to the main view.

Figure 2.3. Screen navigation strip VOICES to LOAD (blue) to SAVE (red) to CV ASSIGN (purple).

TIP Each saved preset remembers its own wavetable. Older presets fall back to the global default wavetable.

2.7 The Options Menu

The options ring lets you change Coral’s performance settings without a computer. Click the encoder past LOAD, SAVE and CV to reach it. Turn to move the orange cursor. A short click toggles a slot or opens a picker sub-view. A slot glowing its own colour is OFF; white means ON. Hold about 1 second to exit, or leave it alone and it closes itself after about 4 seconds.

Coral saves changes straight away. It also writes them into options.txt on the SD card, so the two always agree. You can set the same options in that file instead if you prefer (Chapter 8).

2.8 Drone

Drone is a setting of the part you are on. When it is on, the notes you play keep sounding after you let go of the keys.

Turn drone on and off

1. Open the options ring and select LED 9 (Drone). The drone picker opens.

2. Look at the picker. It shows one LED for each of your 10 engine slots.

3. Click a blue engine. The part changes to that engine and starts to drone.

4. To stop the drone, click the white engine again.

A blue LED is an engine that can drone. A white LED is the engine that this part drones on. When you stop the drone, the held notes fade out with the RELEASE knob.

The encoder selection sets which part the drone applies to. On a part, it applies to that part. On a single voice, it applies to the part of that voice. On ALL, it applies to every part.

How a drone plays

• Nothing sounds until you play a note.

• Play a chord and let go of the keys. The chord keeps sounding.

• The next chord you play replaces the previous chord. You always hear the last chord that you played.

3　MULTIPART AND VOICES

Coral has 8 voices. This chapter shows how to group them into parts. You can then play a mono bassline, a mono lead and a block of polyphonic chords at the same time.

3.1 The Parts Concept

Voices set to the same MIDI channel belong to one part. By default all 8 voices are on MIDI channel 1, so there is a single part. As soon as you assign a voice to a different MIDI channel, a new part is created. Each part can be addressed by its MIDI channel or with the Part CV jack.

Flexibility has a price. We recommend starting with one part. Once comfortable, create two parts and practise switching between them, then build up from there.

How do you know which voice plays a note? Coral assigns a free voice to every MIDI note it receives.

If all voices are busy, it steals the least recently used one. The trigger (Gate) input triggers all voices of the selected part.

3.2 Part and Voice Selection

To navigate voices and parts, push, hold and turn the encoder. From the default state, holding the encoder for half a second lights the ring to show all voices selected. Any change then applies to all voices.

Figure 3.1. Selection sequence: All VOICES selected, PART 1 selected, then VOICE 1, VOICE 2 and on to VOICE 8. Voices occupy LEDs 1 to 8.

• Hold the encoder and turn one tick clockwise to move from All Voices to Part selection.

• Turn another tick to step to voice 1, then voice 2, and so on to voice 8.

• Past voice 8 the selection wraps back to All Voices, then Part selection.

• When more than one part exists, Part selection steps through each part in turn.

• Turning counter-clockwise navigates the other way.

3.3 Creating Parts

This example builds three parts. Voice 1 is a mono bassline on MIDI channel 1. Voice 2 is a mono lead on MIDI channel 2. Voices 3 to 8 are 6-voice polyphonic chords on MIDI channel 3.

1. Set all voices to channel 3 first, so you do not change each voice one by one. Hold the encoder until all voices are selected. Hold the encoder and turn HARM until the ring shows MIDI channel

3. The secondary function of HARM is the MIDI channel. Release the encoder. All voices are now on channel 3, and they form the chords part.

2. Hold the encoder and turn it to voice 1. Hold the encoder and turn HARM until the ring shows MIDI channel 1. Release the encoder. Voice 1 is now its own part.

3. Repeat for voice 2, assigning MIDI channel 2.

During Part selection the three parts now appear. Part 1 is the bassline, Part 2 the lead, and Part 3 the chords and pads.

4　CV AND MIDI MODULATION

There are two sources of modulation: MIDI (CC and Pitch Bend) and the CV inputs. Coral adds the knob position and the CV input to get the value of a voice parameter. The last CC value replaces the knob position. This applies when a CV is assigned to that voice or part.

• Knob value is unipolar, except the bipolar parameters: Pan, Filter envelope and Frequency.

• CV modulation is bipolar: ±5 V.

• CC is unipolar and overrides the knob value.

Parameter value = knob (or CC) + CV modulation.

Each part can be modulated separately, which lets you build richer, more complex sounds.

4.1 CV Modulation

The Atk/Dec, Filter, Harm, Timbre, Morph, Trig, Amp and Oct CV inputs affect the voices of the selected part only. By default there is one part, so all voices respond.

Poly and Trigger Modes (PolyCV)

The PolyCV setting in the options ring sets how CV and the trigger drive the voices. It has six modes:

Mode　Behaviour

0 · Unison　All voices play in unison.

1 · Poly CV　Different CV pitch values trigger different voices. You can play Coral polyphonically from a single Oct CV and one trigger.

2 · Chord hold　Holds a chord across voices.

3 · Chord arp　Arpeggiates the held chord.

4 · Echo　Echo mode.

5 · Echo　Second echo mode.

NOTE In modes 2 to 5, incoming MIDI notes take over the pitch. You can play chords and echoes from a keyboard as well as from CV.

CV Inputs

Input　Effect

Atk/Dec　Increases or decreases attack, decay and release of both the Amp and Mod envelopes. Negative voltages make the sound pluckier, positive voltages softer and longer.

Filter　Positive voltages raise the filter cutoff, negative lower it.

Harm, Timbre, Morph　Positive voltages apply positive modulation on these engine parameters, negative apply negative.

Trig　Triggers the internal envelopes.

Amp　Controls the amplifier level. It scales every engine.

Oct　CV/Oct pitch. The Oct and Frequency (fine) knobs are taken into account for the final pitch.

Part　The voltage on this input selects which part the other CV inputs affect.

The ADSR trimmers also work as bipolar attenuators for the CV inputs below them. Amp Atk scales the Atk/Dec CV. Amp Dec scales the Filter CV. Sust scales the Harm CV. Mod Atk scales the Timbre CV. Mod Dec scales the Morph CV.

4.2 Part CV Input

One way to choose which part the CV modulation affects is the Part CV jack. Only 0 to +5 V is considered. With two parts, the first is addressed between 0 and 2.5 V and the second between 2.5 and 5 V. There is a little hysteresis to avoid jumps at the edges.

4.3 The CV Assign Screen

Leave the Part CV jack unpatched. You can then send the front-panel CV modulation to one part with the CV Assign screen. This is the purple stop in the encoder click cycle. Turn the encoder to choose the part. Click to confirm. Any voltage on the Part CV jack overrides this selection.

Figure 4.1. CV Assign ring: turn to select the part, press to assign and leave.

4.4 MIDI Modulation

With MIDI CC messages you can modulate any parameter inside Coral. Messages are filtered by MIDI channel and applied to the part on that channel. CC is unipolar and overrides the knob value.

5　ENGINES

An engine is the sound generator inside a voice. Coral firmware 3.0 ships 27 engines. You choose any 10 of them when you build your firmware in the Firmware Updater (Chapter 9). The 10 you pick fill the 10 slots on the engine-selection ring, in the order you set. This chapter documents all 27 so you can decide what to load.

NOTE The sampler (WAVPLAYER) is one of the 27 engines, not a separate mode. Some engines are heavier than others, so not every combination of 10 fits. The Updater shows live Flash and RAM meters. It tells you before you build.

The three engine knobs. HARM, TIMBRE and MORPH are Engine Parameters 1, 2 and 3. What they do changes per engine, and is listed with each engine below. Over MIDI they are CC 11, 12 and 13.

5.1 Analog and Subtractive

VIRTUAL ANALOG

Classic two-oscillator subtractive analog. The second oscillator is synced to the first.

Knob　Parameter　Does

HARM　Engine Parameter 1　Oscillator detune, following musical intervals

TIMBRE　Engine Parameter 2　Square shape, from narrow pulse to full square to hard-sync formants

MORPH　Engine Parameter 3　Saw shape, from triangle to saw with a widening notch

3-VCO ANALOG

Three variable-saw oscillators that morph from triangle to saw to square to pulse with dynamic PWM.

Two of the three can be detuned against the main oscillator.

Monophonic SH-101 voice with a sub-oscillator.

TIMBRE　Engine Parameter 2　Waveform and pulse-width

MORPH　Engine Parameter 3　Sub level

Multiple Detuned Oscillator: 8 detuned oscillators per voice morphing between saw, square and PWM.

5.8 Generative Drone

STITCHER

A generative drone looper, and the one engine that plays by its own rules. Stitcher holds a 2 second window of a sample in memory and chops it into three independent loops. Every re-roll rebuilds each loop as a fresh arrangement of slices. The slices use mixed musical lengths, shuffled order, repeats and reversals. Each slice has its own level, pan and pitch. Slices are played like an oscillator rather than gated, so the result flows instead of stuttering.

Read this before you reach for the knobs. On Stitcher the OCT knob is not pitch, and HARM, TIMBRE and MORPH are not the usual engine parameters. They are the levels of the three loops.

Control　On STITCHER

OCT · the big knob　The main control, and not pitch on this engine. Any meaningful move re-rolls the whole arrangement, and its position sets the density. MIDI CC 6 drives it too.

HARM / TIMBRE / MORPH Level of loop 1 / 2 / 3. The three loops are roles rather than copies: percussive, spacey and smeared, so they behave like three different players.

MOD ATK　Bipolar rhythm to texture morph. Centre is neutral. One way gives short slices, rests and a wide pitch spread. The other gives long overlapping slices that sit with the root.

MOD DR　Its normal Coral mod-decay job.

Keys / CV note　Pitch the material. Stitcher is a single-voice texture engine.

Picking a sample

The first encoder click opens the sample browser, shown as a yellow arc. Turn to scrub through the WAV files in your Stitcher folder, then click to exit. Position 0 is the built-in generator, so the engine makes sound even with an empty folder. Your choice is remembered across power cycles.

NOTE Coral creates the Stitcher folder at the root of the SD card on boot, so there is nothing to set up. Copy your WAV files straight into it. That folder at the card root is the only place Stitcher reads, and it does not look inside subfolders. A long file is fine. Each re-roll can take its 2 second window from anywhere in the file. One sample goes a long way.

TIP The Coral Factory package puts a set of sounds in the Stitcher folder (Section 8.1). You can add your own. Stitcher also plays with an empty folder, using its built-in generator at position 0.

The FX ring

A second encoder press opens the Stitcher FX ring: three live toggles you can flip while it plays. A slot at full brightness is on, dim is off. The settings are saved on the device, so they survive a reboot. Hold about 1 second to exit, or leave it and it closes after about 4 seconds.

6　SOUND EFFECTS

There are three effects: Space (reverb), Chorus (ensemble) and Delay. All are send effects common to all voices; the amount depends on each voice level and its send amount.

NOTE The three send amounts and the HP filter cutoff stay with the part when you change its engine. See Section 2.4. Your effects balance survives an engine switch on stage.

6.1 Space

The Space engine is not only a reverb but also improves the stereo image of the dry signal. Send amount is set per voice with SHIFT + FILTER. The size and low-pass of the reverb are set over MIDI (CC 40 and 41).

6.2 Chorus

The chorus is applied per voice. Send amount is set with SHIFT + MORPH when the high-pass filter option is off. Turn on the high-pass filter option and SHIFT + MORPH becomes the per-voice HP cutoff. The chorus send is then not available.

6.3 Delay

The delay is synced to the tempo. Turn on Delay in the options ring (LED 8). SHIFT + TIMBRE then sets the delay send of each voice. It replaces the noise level. Over MIDI, the send is CC 27 on the MIDI channel of the part.

Tempo

The delay follows the MIDI clock on the MIDI input. With no clock, it runs at 120 BPM. After a tempo change, it needs a few seconds to settle. When the clock stops, the delay keeps the last tempo.

7.3 CC and the Panel Pots

A CC takes over the parameter it addresses. The panel pot must catch up before it takes control again. As you turn, the pot and the value meet in the middle. Section 2.2 covers this. It also covers the noccxt setting, which keeps the pots live under a stream of CCs.

This works for every CC in the table above that has a pot. It includes the Space (reverb) and Delay sends. You can automate the sends from your DAW, then pick them up on the panel.

7.4 Program Change

Program Change messages with a value of 1 to 10, received on any MIDI channel, load presets 1 to 10. You can change this in the options ring (Program Change slot): accept all, ignore all, or accept only on an active part channel.

7.5 Pitch Bend

Pitch Bend is applied to the part whose MIDI channel matches the message. The default range is ±2 semitones. You can set it from 1 to 48 with the pbrang option (Chapter 8).

7.6 Glide

Glide is a smooth transition of a voice’s pitch from one note to the next. In polyphonic mode different notes can trigger different voices, so glide can be unpredictable. Use a single-voice (mono) part for a predictable glide. Glide time is CC 7. Glide mode is CC 8: 0 selects glide always, 1 to 127 selects glide on legato only.

7.7 Sustain Pedal

CC 64 acts as a sustain / damper pedal, holding notes and chords while it is down.

7.8 Velocity and Pressure

Note velocity is mapped to level. Channel and polyphonic pressure (aftertouch) modulate the filter cutoff and level for immediate playability.

7.9 MPE

7.3 CC and the Panel Pots

A CC takes over the parameter it addresses. The panel pot must catch up before it takes control again. As you turn, the pot and the value meet in the middle. Section 2.2 covers this. It also covers the noccxt setting, which keeps the pots live under a stream of CCs.

8.3 options.txt

options.txt is a plain-text file in the System folder, created on first boot. Every setting Coral has lives here, one per line: a six-letter key, a space, then a value (usually 1 for on and 0 for off). Order does not matter. You can edit it on a computer with any text editor.

The SD card owns your settings. Coral reads them from the card at boot. Only you change them, in this file or on the options ring. Updating the firmware never alters them.

Which settings the file owns, and which the ring owns

Most of these settings can also be changed on the Coral itself, on the options ring (Chapter 2). The two work together, with one simple rule.

- **Ring options are in the file too.** Whenever you toggle one on the ring, Coral refreshes options.txt to match. While you are playing, the ring is in charge.
- **Your edits win.** If you edit options.txt on a computer, your version is used on the next boot. So the file is always a safe way to set things up.
- **Some settings are file only.** vumetr, ledalw, extpre, obvspr, pbrang, noccxt, devfsh and engcol have no place on the ring. You set them here only.

TIP Upgrading from firmware 2.6? Your old options.txt works exactly as it did. polycv, encpri and cvpart are normal keys again, so a 2.6 file is read verbatim.

9 COMPANION WEB APPS

Three free web apps support Coral, Firmware Updater, Preset Manager and Waveform. All run in your browser. The Firmware Updater builds and flashes firmware, the Preset Manager builds and manages presets, and the Waveform Generator makes wavetables.

9.1 Firmware Updater

The Firmware Updater does three things. You choose your 10 engines or less. The OXI build server compiles a custom firmware. You flash it to Coral over USB. Use Chrome or Edge, which support WebUSB.

Step 1 · Put Coral in update mode

Hold the BOOT button on the Daisy board inside the module. Connect Coral to the computer by USB. It appears as a DFU device. Power it from USB only, with nothing else connected.

Step 2 · Connect

Click Connect Coral and select the DFU device. The app can read back and show the firmware currently installed.

Step 3 · Build or choose firmware

- Start from a shipped layout in the preset menu, or pick your own 10 engines in the grid. The chosen engines fill the 10 slots in order.
- Watch the Flash and RAM meters. Green means it will build. Some engines are large (FMX7, PIANOZ and STITCHER especially), so a combination of several heavy engines may not fit. The meters tell you before you build.
- Leave WAVPLAYER out of your 10 and Coral drops the sampler from the build. Its memory comes back. That leaves room for heavier engines.
- Your settings are never touched. Flashing changes the firmware only: your options live on the SD card and are read from there on the next boot.
- Click Build firmware. Every build compiles a fresh firmware on the server. You can also save your 10-engine layout as a .json file to reload or share. You can print a one-page cheat sheet for your build.

NOTE Instead of building, you can switch to the Upload .bin tab and flash a .bin you already have.

Step 4 · Flash

Do not unplug the module while it flashes. Click Flash to Coral and wait. Coral restarts on the new firmware when it finishes.

CAUTION Flashing replaces the firmware, not your SD card. Your presets, samples and wavetables stay on the card. If you added an engine that needs files on the card, make sure they are there. PIANOZ needs HOUSEKEYS.PCM and RHODES.PCM in System/. FMX7 needs its DX7 banks (Section 8.1).

10　CALIBRATION

Calibrate the CV/Oct tracking if pitch drifts. You need a well-calibrated ±1 V source.

1. Turn Amp Atk, Amp Dr, Sust, Mod Atk, Mod Dr and F.Reso fully clockwise, and the F.Env trimmer fully counter-clockwise.

2. Unplug all patch cables from the module.

3. Hold the encoder for 5 seconds until the ring shows the green pattern.

4. Tap the encoder; the ring turns red.

5. Patch the OCT CV input and send -1 V from a well-calibrated source. (On the OXI One, C1 outputs -1 V.)

6. Tap the encoder once; the ring shows red and amber.

7. Send +1 V to the OCT input and tap the encoder again. (On the OXI One, C3 outputs +1 V.)

8. Tap the encoder again. If it worked, the green confirmation animation appears.

NOTE Depending on your voltage source, -1 V may correspond to a different MIDI note.

10.1 Fix Tuning If You Only Use MIDI

This fix is for MIDI only. Use it if your Coral plays out of tune after installing 3.0. In that case its calibration file was replaced by the one in the old Factory package. You can fix it in one minute, with no cables.

1. Unplug every cable from the Coral's CV inputs. Leave MIDI connected if you want.

2. Turn Amp Atk, Amp Dr, Sust, Mod Atk, Mod Dr and F.Reso fully clockwise, and the F.Env trimmer fully counter-clockwise.

3. Hold the encoder down for about 5 seconds, until the LEDs turn cyan and white.

4. Click the encoder 3 times, waiting a second between clicks. The LEDs change colour after each click.

5. After the third click the LEDs light up. This is normal: the Coral has already saved the fix.

6. Turn the Coral off and on again.

Your Coral now plays in tune from MIDI. Set your knobs back where you like them.

NOTE This fix does not calibrate the OCT CV input. If you play Coral from CV/Oct, use the full calibration above with a well-calibrated ±1 V source.

B　APPENDIX: TROUBLESHOOTING

Symptom　What to do

MIDI stops responding until I power cycle, but the sound keeps playing

Update to firmware 3.0. A single corrupted MIDI byte could lock up the MIDI input on older firmware. A worn cable or connector produces one sooner or later. Audio carried on, so the module looked frozen while it still droned. Firmware 3.0 recovers from a corrupted byte at once. If it continues after you update, try a different MIDI cable.

Coral freezes and only a power cycle brings it back

Check the SD card. A card can refuse writes when it is write-protected, worn out, or has a damaged filesystem. Older firmware then kept retrying the save of your settings, and stopped responding while it did. Firmware 3.0 gives up after a few tries instead of hanging. Make sure the card is not write-protected. Copy your content to a fresh card if you think it is failing.

No sound at all　Make sure the Micro SD card is in the slot. Make sure the part you play is on the MIDI channel you send. Make sure the voice level is up. Hold the encoder for 5 seconds to return Coral to its default state (Section 3.4).

One engine is silent while the others play

That engine may need files on the SD card. PIANOZ needs

HOUSEKEYS.PCM and RHODES.PCM in System/, and FMX7 needs its DX7 banks. Copy the Coral Factory package to the card (Section 8.1).

Seeing the folders on the card is not enough: the files must be inside them.

Some of my samples do not show up, or Coral takes a long time to start

Update to firmware 3.0. Older firmware read a large piece of every WAV while it scanned the card. That made start-up slow on a full card. It could also leave files out of the list. Firmware 3.0 reads only what it needs.

Start-up is much quicker, and it finds every playable file.

Clicks or artifacts from the sampler

Crackle or dropouts with several sampler voices at once is a different thing. That is card speed. Use a fast card (U3). Convert samples to 48 kHz 16-bit. Use fewer voices on the sampler at once (Section 5.9).

A pot does nothing until I turn it a long way

It is catching up with a value set over MIDI, or by a part or preset change: keep turning and the value comes to meet you. Section 2.2 explains this, and noccxt can stop CCs arming catch-up at all.

Pitch is off when playing from CV

Calibrate the CV/Oct input (Chapter 10).

My Stitcher samples disappeared

Stitcher reads only the Stitcher folder at the root of the card. Move your WAV files there (Section 5.8).
